summary: Defines a general framework for the metrics developed by the IETF's IP Performance Metrics effort. It lays out concepts and methods so that measurements of things like delay and packet loss are defined clearly and can be compared.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2330 sets the ground rules for measuring Internet performance, such as delay and packet loss. It defines shared terms, says how metrics must be specified, and explains how to collect and check measurement data. Because of this framework, two teams measuring the same path can compare their results.

questions: what is wire time in network measurement
subtitle: The shared vocabulary and rules that let Internet performance measurements mean the same thing to everyone.

tldr.problem: The IETF's IP Performance Metrics effort needed shared rules so that measurements of Internet paths and clouds are accurate, repeatable and understood the same way by users and providers.
tldr.mechanism: The framework defines terms for paths, clouds, clocks and wire time, sets criteria for metrics, and prescribes how to collect and check samples, recommending Poisson sampling and deterministic definitions.
tldr.outcome: The framework shaped the IPPM metric specifications that followed it; RFC 2330 is Informational and has been updated by RFC 7312, RFC 8468 and RFC 9198.

sections.title: Purpose and Criteria for Metrics
sections.content:
This memo defines a general framework for the metrics developed by the IETF's IP Performance Metrics (IPPM) effort, begun by the Benchmarking Methodology Working Group and continued by the IPPM Working Group. The overarching goal is a situation in which users and providers of Internet transport service share an accurate understanding of the performance and reliability of the network clouds they use or provide.

The criteria the RFC lists for such metrics: they must be concrete and well-defined. Their methodology should be repeatable, giving the same measurements under identical conditions. They must show no bias for IP clouds built with identical technology, and understood and fair bias for clouds built with non-identical technology. They must be useful to users and providers, and they must avoid inducing artificial performance goals.

The memo also warns that passages in braces, written as {Comment: ...}, are commentary only. They illustrate points but are not part of the framework and do not propose particular metrics.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF wanted Internet performance numbers to mean the same thing to everyone. This memo sets the rules those numbers must follow, so measurements stay honest and comparable.

sections.title: Paths, Clouds and Exchanges
sections.content:
The framework defines precise vocabulary for network pieces. A host is a computer that speaks the Internet protocols, including routers. A link is a single link-level connection between two or more hosts, such as a leased line, an Ethernet or a frame relay cloud. A router is a host that forwards IP packets.

A path is a one-way sequence of hosts and links, written as a list from a starting host h0 to an ending host hn, where the hosts in between are routers; a link together with the host it reaches is a hop. A subpath is any part of a path that is itself a path. A cloud is an undirected graph whose vertices are routers and whose edges are links; connecting to a cloud means connecting to one of its routers over a link, and that link is not part of the cloud. An exchange is a special link that connects a host to a cloud or one cloud to another.

Two derived terms follow. A cloud subpath is a subpath all of whose hosts are routers of one cloud. A path digest compresses a path into hosts connected by exchanges and cloud subpaths, so large stretches of a path can be treated as single pieces.
sections.plainLanguage: Before measuring anything, everyone needs the same words for the pieces: a path is a one-way chain of hosts and links, and a cloud is a group of routers linked together.

sections.title: Metrics, Methodologies and Frameworks
sections.content:
A carefully specified quantity of interest is a metric. A metric may be hard to measure in practice, and that is allowed; ambiguity in meaning is not. Metrics use standard units: meters or seconds with thousandth and thousand prefixes such as km, ms and us, the bit as the unit of information, decimal (1000-based) prefixes with bits, and UTC for times. Some metrics are defined purely in terms of other metrics; these are derived metrics.

A measurement methodology is how a metric is obtained, for example direct measurement with injected test traffic, projection from lower-level measurements, or estimation from aggregated measurements. A methodology should be repeatable, and the RFC introduces continuity: small changes in conditions should cause small changes in results. Methodologies should also strive to minimise, document and quantify their uncertainties, such as clock errors, and some are conservative, meaning the act of measurement barely changes what is measured.

Metrics that fit the Internet's common analytical framework, the set of concepts engineers use for design, simulation and analysis, are analytically specified metrics. Metrics that do not fit that framework, such as the best flow capacity achievable along a path using a compliant TCP, are empirically specified metrics: they are pinned down by describing a reference methodology for measuring them. The framework also allows spatial composition, relating a path metric to the same metric on its subpaths, and temporal composition, relating a metric at one time to its values at other times.
sections.plainLanguage: A metric says exactly what quantity is meant. A methodology says how it is measured. When a quantity cannot be derived from first principles, the RFC pins it down by specifying how to measure it instead.

sections.title: Clocks and Wire Time
sections.content:
Time measurement is at the heart of many Internet metrics, so the framework adopts clock terminology from the Network Time Protocol (RFC 1305). A clock's offset is the difference between the time it reports and true UTC time. Accuracy is how close that offset is to zero. Skew is the frequency difference between the clock and true time, and drift is variation in that skew. Resolution is the smallest unit by which the clock updates, a lower bound on its uncertainty. When two clocks are compared, the terms gain relatives: relative offset between them, joint resolution as the sum of both resolutions, and synchronized clocks are ones whose relative offset is zero. For many measurements, synchronization between the two clocks matters more than either clock's accuracy: the RFC's example is a transcontinental one-way delay of about 50 ms, where a skew of 0.01% adds 60 ms of error after 10 minutes, which can wipe out the measurement.

The memo also defines wire time, to separate network behaviour from the delays hosts themselves introduce. For a packet P observed by a host H on a link L, the wire arrival time is the first time any bit of P appears at H's position on L, and the wire exit time is the first time all its bits have appeared. Metrics should be defined in terms of wire times rather than host endpoint times, so the definition separates host delays from network delays.

The RFC notes practical clock hazards. Synchronizing indirectly over the network with a protocol such as NTP is unsound when the Internet paths involved are the very properties being measured. And a clock set forward or backward during synchronization can break the assumption that timestamps increase.
sections.plainLanguage: Measurements rely on clocks, and clocks lie in specific ways: a fixed offset, a wrong speed, and coarse ticks. The framework names each way, and defines wire time as the moment a packet passes a point on the cable, not the moment a program notices it.

sections.title: Singletons, Samples and Statistics
sections.content:
The framework separates three notions. A singleton is one atomic instance of a metric, such as one bulk throughput measurement. A sample gathers many distinct instances of a singleton, such as an hour of one-way delay measurements. A statistical metric computes a statistic, such as the mean, over a sample. Keeping these apart lets lessons about sampling and statistics be reused across metrics.

On collecting samples, periodic sampling is simple but has two problems: it can lock onto periodic behaviour in the network, and it can be anticipated and manipulated, while repeated identical perturbations can synchronise the network. The sounder approach is random additive sampling with independent random intervals. The RFC generally prefers Poisson sampling, where intervals follow an exponential distribution with rate lambda, so new samples cannot be predicted and the sample stays unbiased even when measuring perturbs the network. Geometric sampling, which records each event with a fixed probability, shares those properties. The RFC gives three methods for generating Poisson intervals, trading implementation difficulty against error, and warns that the time a measurement itself takes must be accounted for.

Two further disciplines close the section. Self-consistency checks test assumptions: a round-trip time that comes out negative flags a bug, and a line fitted to delay samples over time reveals clock skew. And for describing samples, the RFC standardises the empirical distribution function, F(x) as the fraction of measurements at or below x, with percentiles read from it; any percentile summary must report the sample size N, because differences finer than 1/N are below the sample's resolution.
sections.plainLanguage: One measurement is a singleton, a batch of them is a sample, and an average over the batch is a statistic. Take samples at random times, not fixed ones, and check your own results for signs that the method itself is broken.

sections.title: Conventions for Defining Metrics
sections.content:
The framework sets naming and definitional conventions. Metrics should be defined deterministically, not stochastically: a packet loss rate, not a packet loss probability, because probabilities smuggle in hidden assumptions, such as assuming queueing drops are random when they are usually deterministic. Probabilities may still be estimated from measurements afterwards.

Because a metric's value can depend on the type of packet used, the framework introduces the packet of type P: a metric name must include the type, or the phrase type-P, as in IP-type-P-connectivity. Endpoints should be named by IP addresses, not host names, since a host can sit on several networks; the start of a unidirectional path is Src and the end is Dst.

Unless stated otherwise, metric definitions assume standard-formed packets: the IP length field matches header plus payload, the header is valid with version 4 and header length of at least 5, the packet is not fragmented, source and destination addresses match the hosts in question, the TTL is sufficient for the trip or is the maximum of 255, there are no IP options, and any transport header is valid. A packet length B satisfies 0 to 65535 octets. The smallest useful reference packet, the minimal IP packet from A to B, is standard-formed with a zero-octet payload and no options. The Security Considerations section notes that active measurement traffic can be abused for denial-of-service attacks and passive recording can expose traffic contents, so every metric definition must include its own discussion of security.
sections.plainLanguage: Define metrics as counts and rates, not probabilities. Name the exact packet type and the IP addresses involved, and assume packets are well formed unless you say otherwise.

items.title: Offset
items.text: Reported time minus true UTC time.

items.title: Accuracy
items.text: How close the offset is to zero.

items.title: Resolution
items.text: Smallest step in the clock's reported time.

items.title: Joint resolution
items.text: Sum of two clocks' resolutions; a lower bound on interval accuracy.
